d: 1. In the neighborhood of; near or next to; not far from; close to; along with; as, come and sit by me. By foundation or by shady rivulet He sought them both. Milton.
2. On; along; in traversing. Compare 5. Long labors both by sea and land he bore. Dryden. By land, by water, they renew the charge. Pope.
3. Near to, while passing; hence, from one to the other side of; past; as, to go by a church.
4. Used in specifying adjacent dimensions; as, a cabin twenty feet by forty.
5. Against. [Obs.] Tyndale [1. Cor. iv. 4].
6. With, as means, way, process, etc.; through means of; with aid of; through; through the act or agency of; as, a city is destroyed by fire; profit is made by commerce; to take by force.
w.e: OE. bi, AS. bi, big, near to, by, of, from, after, according to; akin to OS.& OFries. bi, be, D. bij, OHG. bi, G. bie, Goth. bi, and perh. Gr.. E. prefix be- is orig.the same word. pref. Be-.

d: 1. Near; in the neighborhood; present; as, there was no person by at the time.
2. Passing near; going past; past; beyond; as, the procession has gone by; a bird flew by.
3. Aside; as, to lay by; to put by.

Out of the common path; aside; -- used in composition, giving the meaning of something aside, secondary, or incidental, or collateral matter, a thing private or avoiding notice; as, by-line, by-place, by-play, by-street. It was formerly more freely used in composition than it is now; as, by-business, by-concernment, by- design, by-interest, etc.

n: so as to pass a given point
every hour a train goes past
started setting aside money to buy a car

d: A piece of leather crossing the breast, used by the men who drag sledges in coal mines.
One who bids at an auction in behalf of the auctioneer or owner, for the purpose of running up the price of articles. [U.S.]
1. A side or incidental blow; an accidental blow. With their by-blows they did split the very stones in pieces. Bunyan.
2. An illegitimate child; a bastard. The Aga speedily . . . brought her [his disgraced slave] to court, together with her pretty by-blow, the present Padre Ottomano. Evelyn.
A private corner. Britain being a by-corner, out of the road of the world. Fuller.
An appendage; that which depends on something else, or is distinct from the main dependence; an accessory. Shak.
A drinking between meals. [Obs.]

1. A thing not directly aimed at; something which is a secondary object of regard; an object by the way, etc.; as in on or upon the bye, i.e., in passing; indirectly; by implication. [Obs. except in the phrase by the bye.] The Synod of Dort condemneth upon the bye even the discipline of the Church of England. Fuller.
2. (Cricket) “A run made upon a missed ball; as, to steal a bye. T. Hughes. By the bye, in passing; by way of digression; apropos to the matter in hand. [Written also by the by.]”
b, to dwell sq. root97.]
1. A dwelling. Gibson.
2. In certain games, a station or place of an individual player. Emerson.

n: an automatic advance to the next round in a tournament without playing an opponent
he had a bye in the first round

d: An election held by itself, not at the time of a general election.

n: a special election between regular elections

d: Private end or interest; secret purpose; selfish advantage. [Written also bye-end.] Profit or some other by-end. L'Estrange.
Past; gone by. Bygone fooleries. Shak
Something gone by or past; a past event. Let old bygones be Tennyson. Let bygones be bygones, let the past be forgotten.

n: past events to be put aside

d: Self-interest; private advantage. Atterbury.
A peninsula. [Obs.]
See Bilander.[Obs.]
A private lane, or one opening out of the usual road.

1. A local or subordinate law; a private law or regulation made by a corporation for its own government. There was likewise a law to restrain the by-laws, or ordinances of corporations. Bacon. The law or institution; to which are added two by-laws, as a comment upon the general law. Addison.

2. A law that is less important than a general law or constitutional provision, and subsidiary to it; a rule relating to a matter of detail; as, civic societies often adopt a constitution and by-laws for the government of their members. In this sense the word has probably been influenced by by, meaning secondary or aside.
w.e: Cf.Sw.bylag, D.bylov, Icel.b, fr.Sw.& Dan. by town, Icel. bær, byr (fr. bûa to dwell) + the word for law; hence, a law for one town, a special law. Cf.Birlaw and see Law.

n: a rule adopted by an organization in order to regulate its own affairs and the behavior of its members

d: To give a nickname to. Camden.

n: a familiar name for a person (often a shortened version of a person's given name)

d: A passage different from the usual one; a byway.
Past; gone by. By-past perils. Shak.
A retired or private place.
Action carried on aside, and commonly in dumb show, while the main action proceeds.

d: A secondary or additional product; something produced, as in the course of a manufacture, in addition to the principal product.

d: A cow house. [N. of Eng.& Scot.]
w.e: Cf, Icel. bür pantry, Sw. bur cage,Dan. buur, E.bower.

d: Private end or view; by-interest. [Obs.] Dryden.

n: a side road little traveled (as in the countryside)

d: Pertaining to, or in the style of, Lord Byron. With despair and Byronic misanthropy. Thackeray
A private room or apartment. Stand in some by-room Shak.

d: Byssaceous.
1. A cloth of exceedingly fine texture, used by the ancients. It is disputed whether it was of cotton, linen, or silk. [Written also byss and byssin.]

2. (Zoöl.) “A tuft of long, tough filaments which are formed in a groove of the foot, and issue from between the valves of certain bivalve mollusks, as the Pinna and Mytilus, by which they attach themselves to rocks, etc.”
3. (Bot.) “An obsolete name for certain fungi composed of slender threads.”
4. Asbestus.

n: tuft of strong filaments by which e.g. a mussel makes itself fast to a fixed surface

d: One who stands near; a spectator; one who has no concern with the business transacting. He addressed the bystanders and scattered pamphlets among them. Palfrey.
w.e: By + stander, equiv. to stander-by; cf. AS. big-standan to stand by or near.

d: A separate, private, or obscure street; an out of the way or cross street. He seeks by-streets, and saves the expensive coach. Gay.
An accidental or a slyly given stroke.
An obscure road; a way turning from the main road. Sir P. Sidney.
A private or selfish view; self-interested aim or purpose. No by-views of his own shall mislead him. Atterbury.
secluded or private walk. He moves afterward in by-walks. Dryden.
The outlet from a dam or reservoir; also, a cut to divert the flow of water.
A secluded, private, or obscure way; a path or road aside from the main one. Take no byways. Herbert.

n: a side road little traveled (as in the countryside)

d: A secret or side stroke, as of raillery or sarcasm. Milton.
1. A common saying; a proverb; a saying that has a general currency. I knew a wise man that had it for a byword. Bacon.

n: a condensed but memorable saying embodying some important fact of experience that is taken as true by many people

d: Work aside from regular work; subordinate or secondary business.
